say: You give it a list of numbers, or a **frequency table**. It gives back three ways to say what is typical: the mean, the median and the mode.
The key idea: the mean shares the total out equally, the median is the middle value once the data is in order, and the mode is the value that turns up most.

how.higher: Higher level uses it inside Paper 2 statistics questions, and three parts test it as the main skill: you are given a mean, median or mode and must find a missing value.
how.ordinary: Ordinary level tests it almost every year on Paper 2, usually as a short part of 5 to 10 marks: a mean from a frequency table, a median with a reason, or a missing value from a given mean.

example.question:
The table shows the number of books 20 students read last month.
Books read, $x$: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
Number of students, $f$: 2, 3, 6, 4, 5
Find the mean, the median and the mode.

steps.title: Count the students
steps.say: The frequencies tell you how many values there are. Add them to find $n$.

steps.title: Find the mean
steps.say: Multiply each value by its frequency and add. Then divide by $n$ to get the $\hl{1}{\text{mean}}$.

steps.title: Find the median
steps.say: There are $20$ values, so the $\hl{2}{\text{median}}$ is halfway between the 10th and the 11th. Add the frequencies as you go to find where they sit.

lines.text: Running total: $2, 5, 11, 15, 20$. The 10th and 11th values are both in the group for $x = 3$.

steps.title: Find the mode
steps.say: The $\hl{3}{\text{mode}}$ is the value with the biggest frequency.

higher.tip: A part with several values to find is marked value by value. Find as many as you can, because each correct one earns marks on its own.

sources.quote: Work of merit in finding one value

higher.tip: A correct final value earns full marks even with no working, but only if it is right. Show working in case it is not.

sources.quote: Full credit for correct answers without work
Accept correct answer without work in (i)

ordinary.tip: Write out the mean formula with your numbers in it. Writing it fully substituted earns high partial credit even if the arithmetic goes wrong.
When asked for the median, say what it means. The explanation is a mark of its own: half the values are above it and half below.
Round as the question asks and say so. A wrong or missing rounding costs a mark.
For a short part like finding the range, a correct answer with no working still gets full marks.

say: You give it a set of data. It gives back a **graph** that shows the data clearly: bar chart, pie chart, line plot, histogram or stem-and-leaf.
The key idea: each item must be drawn in proportion to its size. For a pie chart that means sharing $360^\circ$ out in proportion to the frequencies.

how.ordinary: Ordinary level asks for it on Paper 2 almost every year, 16 times as the main skill: draw a pie chart, bar chart or histogram, worth 5 to 15 marks, often with the working out of angles or heights as a separate part.

example.question:
60 students were asked how they travel to school.
Bus: 24, Car: 18, Walk: 12, Cycle: 6
Find the angle for each sector of a pie chart of this data.

steps.title: Angle for one student
steps.say: A pie chart is a full circle, $360^\circ$, shared among all $60$ students. Divide to find the angle for one student.

steps.title: Check the total
steps.say: The sectors must fill the circle. Add the angles and check you get $360^\circ$.

lines.text: Now draw each sector with a protractor and label it with its group name.

ordinary.tip: Label every sector or bar. Leaving a label off costs a mark, even when the drawing is right.
Start by finding the total number of items. That step alone earns partial credit toward the angles.
Round percentages and angles correctly. Missing or wrong rounding costs a mark.

sources.quote: Apply a * for no or incorrect rounding

ordinary.tip: For a histogram, get every interval drawn at the right height. Four correct intervals earns high partial credit.

say: You give it a population and a way of picking people from it. It tells you whether the sample is a **simple random sample**, and if not, where the bias comes from.
The key idea: in a simple random sample every member has the same chance of being picked. If some people are more likely to be picked, or left out, the sample is biased.

how.ordinary: Ordinary level tested it once as the main skill, on Paper 2 in 2023: say why a sample could be unrepresentative, as part of a 10 mark part.

example.question:
A school has 600 students. The principal wants to survey 30 of them about the canteen. She asks the first 30 students who arrive at school in the morning.
Give one reason this sample could be biased. Describe how to pick a simple random sample of 30 instead.

steps.title: Spot the bias
steps.say: Ask who could never be picked. The students who arrive late have no chance, so the sample is not **representative**.

lines.text: Early arrivals may come by school bus or eat breakfast at school. Their views on the canteen may differ from the rest.

steps.title: Number the population
steps.say: A simple random sample needs a full list. Give every student a number from $1$ to $600$.

lines.text: The list is the whole population.

steps.title: Pick at random
steps.say: Use a random number generator or draw numbers from a hat. Pick $30$ different numbers. Those students are the sample.

lines.text: The principal does not choose. Chance decides.

steps.title: Check it is fair
steps.say: Every student must have the same chance of being picked. Work out the chance.

workedSolution.finalAnswer: \text{Biased: late arrivals cannot be picked. Fix: number all 600, pick 30 at random, each chance } \frac{1}{20}

ordinary.tip: To explain bias, say the sample may not be representative of everyone.
Name who is left out. Saying that later arrivals have no chance of being picked is an accepted answer.

sources.quote: Leaves out students who arrive later to school

say: You give it a description of a study. It names the type: a **survey**, an observational study or a designed experiment.
The key idea: ask whether the researcher changed anything. A survey asks questions, an observational study only watches, and an experiment assigns people to different treatments.

example.question:
A researcher wants to know if a new fertiliser makes tomato plants grow taller. She splits 40 plants at random into two equal groups. One group gets the fertiliser and the other does not. After 6 weeks she measures every plant.
What type of study is this? Give a reason.

steps.title: Did she change anything?
steps.say: Ask whether the researcher gave something to the subjects. Here she gave fertiliser to one group only.

lines.text: She applied a treatment. A survey or an observational study never does.

steps.title: Were groups made at random?
steps.say: In an experiment, chance decides who gets the treatment. This keeps the groups alike.

lines.text: Plants were split at random into two groups.

steps.title: Find the group size
steps.say: The groups are equal, so share the plants out evenly.

lines.text: Each group has $20$ plants. One is the treatment group and one is the comparison group.

steps.title: Name the type
steps.say: She applied a treatment to randomly chosen groups and compared the results.

workedSolution.finalAnswer: \text{Designed experiment: treatment given to random groups of } 20
